Lighthouses: A Short History of Light on the Coast

By Tobias Weir. Updated 2 April 2026.

Why the coast needed a light

For most of history, the sea was crossed in daylight and in sight of land. Sailors steered by headlands, church towers and hills, and they anchored for the night rather than risk the rocks. As trade grew and ships began to sail through the dark, the most dangerous part of any voyage became the last few miles, where a ship came close to the shore it was trying to reach. Reefs, sandbars and rocky points claimed vessels in huge numbers, and the harbours that lost the most ships had the strongest reason to build something that could be seen from far away at night. The first answer was the simplest one: a fire on a hill. Over many centuries that fire grew into a tower, then a tower with a lamp, and finally a precise optical machine. The story of the lighthouse is the story of how people learned to turn a small amount of light into a signal that could be read from many miles out to sea.

The Pharos of Alexandria

The most famous early lighthouse stood on the island of Pharos, at the entrance to the harbour of Alexandria in Egypt. It was built in the third century BC during the reign of the Ptolemies, and ancient writers counted it among the wonders of the world. Accounts differ on its exact height, but all agree that it was far taller than any other building of its kind and could be seen from a long way off. A fire burned at the top, and a polished surface is said to have reflected its glow toward the sea. The tower survived for well over a thousand years, damaged by a series of earthquakes, until the last of it fell in the fourteenth century. The word for lighthouse in several languages, including French and Italian, still comes from the name of the island, which shows how strongly the building shaped the idea of what a lighthouse is.

Open fires and coal beacons

For nearly two thousand years after the Pharos, most lighthouses were little more than iron baskets of burning wood or coal on top of a tower. They were hungry for fuel. A coal beacon could burn through many tons in a single winter, and the fuel had to be carried up the tower by hand. The light they gave was poor: smoke and sparks blew across the flame, rain and wind could put it out, and the glow from a coal fire was dull compared with a good lamp. Even so, a fire on a tower was far better than darkness, and ports competed to keep theirs lit. Many were paid for by a tax on passing ships, which sometimes led to quarrels over who should pay and who should keep the light. A fire that went out on a stormy night could cost lives, and a keeper who let the fuel run low might be fined or dismissed.

The Eddystone problem

Building a lighthouse on land is hard enough, but the most dangerous rocks lie well offshore, where the sea breaks over them in every storm. The Eddystone Rocks, about fourteen miles off the coast of Plymouth in England, were a notorious trap for ships entering the English Channel. The first tower there was a wooden structure begun in 1696 by Henry Winstanley, and it was swept away in a great storm in 1703 with Winstanley inside it. A second tower, built by John Rudyerd, lasted until it burned down in 1755. The third, built by John Smeaton and finished in 1759, changed the field. Smeaton studied the shape of an oak tree, which is wide at the base and narrows as it rises, and cut his granite blocks to lock together like dovetailed joints. His tower stood for more than a century, and its design was copied around the world.

Argand lamps and reflectors

Better towers needed better lamps. In the 1780s the Swiss scientist Aime Argand invented an oil lamp with a hollow circular wick, which let air reach the flame from both inside and out. The result burned far brighter and cleaner than an ordinary wick, and lighthouse builders soon adopted it. They placed these lamps in front of curved metal mirrors, usually made of silvered copper, to throw the light in one direction instead of letting it spread. Scotland's Stevenson family of engineers, who built many of the country's lighthouses, including the Bell Rock light in 1810, used such lamps and mirrors extensively. The system worked, but it needed constant polishing, because soot dulled the mirrors, and a lot of light was still lost around the edges. The next step came from a French physicist who looked at the problem in an entirely new way.

Fresnel's lens

In the 1820s the French engineer Augustin Fresnel designed a lens made of many glass rings and prisms arranged around a central lamp. A solid glass lens large enough to gather the light of a lighthouse lamp would have been too heavy to build or turn. Fresnel's stepped design kept only the parts of the glass that actually bend the light, and it made the lens thin and light. It captured much more of the lamp's output and sent it out as a narrow, powerful beam. The first Fresnel lens was installed at the Cordouan lighthouse in France in 1823, and within a few decades the design had spread to nearly every major light. Lenses came in sizes called orders, from the huge first order, taller than a person, down to small sixth order lenses for harbours. Many are still in use today, and a few still turn on their original mechanisms.

The keeper's life

Behind every lamp was a keeper, and often a family. A keeper's day was built around the light. In the evening the lamp was lit and the lens set turning, during the night someone had to watch it, trim the wick or refill the oil, and in the morning the glass was cleaned and the brass polished. A clockwork motor that drove the lens had to be wound by hand every few hours, so no keeper could sleep through a whole night. Remote stations were isolated for weeks, and rock towers were reached only by boat in calm weather. Supplies, letters and relief crews came on a schedule that the weather often ignored. Keepers wrote logbooks recording the weather, passing ships and any wrecks, and many of these logs survive as a valuable record of coastal life. The work was lonely and sometimes dangerous, but it was also respected, and keepers took pride in never letting a light go out.

Fog signals and sound

Light is useless in fog, so lighthouses also learned to make noise. The earliest fog signals were simple bells struck by hand or by a clockwork hammer, and some stations fired a cannon at fixed intervals. In the nineteenth century engineers built steam whistles, large trumpets driven by compressed air, and sirens that could be heard for miles. Each station had its own pattern of blasts, so that a ship in fog could tell which signal it was hearing. Sound behaves oddly over water, however, and a ship might hear a signal clearly in one place and not at all a short distance away. Mariners learned to treat sound as a hint rather than a guarantee. In the twentieth century fog signals began to be replaced by electronic horns and then by radio beacons, and many of the old sirens were switched off for good.

Reading a light: characters and colours

No two neighbouring lights should look the same, and the system of light characters makes sure of it. A light may be fixed, shining steadily, or flashing, with a short light and a long dark period, or occulting, with a long light and a short dark. Others show groups of flashes, such as two flashes followed by a pause. Each light has a period, the time it takes to complete one cycle, and a colour, usually white, red or green. Navigation charts list these details for every light, and a navigator who sees a flash group on the horizon can time it with a watch and compare it with the chart. Some lights are divided into sectors of different colours, which warn of hidden dangers: a ship in the white sector is on a safe course, while red or green warns that it is drifting toward trouble. The nominal range printed on the chart assumes clear weather and is only a guide.

Radio, radar and satellites

For most of the twentieth century, lighthouses were joined by newer aids. Radio beacons transmitted signals that a ship could use to find its bearing, radar let a ship see coastlines and other vessels in the dark, and later systems based on satellites gave a position fixed to within a few metres. By the 1990s, GPS receivers were cheap enough that small boats carried them, and the satellite fix quickly became the main way ships found their position. Commercial shipping also adopted electronic charts and automatic identification systems that show nearby vessels on a screen. These tools were so much more precise than a light on a distant tower that some people asked whether lighthouses had become obsolete. Most authorities decided to keep them, as a backup that works without electronics, and as a landmark that a sailor can still trust when a screen fails.

Automation and the end of the keeper

Once electric lamps and automatic controls became reliable, the keeper's job began to disappear. A light sensor can switch the lamp on at dusk, a spare bulb can rotate into place when one fails, and a radio link can report faults to a distant office. Governments, tired of the cost of staffing remote towers, began to automate lights in the twentieth century. In Britain, the last lighthouse with a keeper, at North Foreland in Kent, was automated in 1998, and most other countries followed the same path. A few stations kept people on site for tradition or tourism, and in the United States, Boston Light remains staffed. The change saved money and removed a dangerous job, but it also ended a way of life, and the families who had lived at the stations moved away.

Saving the towers

With keepers gone and the lights automated, many towers were left empty and began to decay. Salt, wind and damp attack stone and iron, and a tower that is not maintained can fall into ruin within a few decades. Communities, charities and governments have since taken up the task of saving the best of them. Some towers have become museums, others hold hotels or holiday lets, and some are looked after by volunteer groups who open them to visitors on summer weekends. Moving a tower is also possible: in 1999 the Cape Hatteras lighthouse in North Carolina, the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, was lifted onto rails and moved about 2,900 feet inland to save it from the eroding shore. Whatever the future of navigation holds, the lighthouse has become a symbol that people want to keep, and its towers will remain on the coast long after their original job is done.
